title: Juice Uses Earth’s Gravity to Help It Reach Jupiter
summary:
The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, known as Juice, passed Earth on September 28, 2026. The spacecraft used Earth’s gravity to change its route toward Jupiter while using very little fuel.

This kind of move is called a gravity assist. A planet’s gravity can help change a spacecraft’s speed and direction. During this flyby, Juice’s direction changed by 20 degrees, and its speed increased by 3.5 kilometres per second.

At its closest point, Juice was 8,640 kilometres above the Indian Ocean. Its monitoring cameras took a series of pictures during the encounter.

Reaching the right path required careful planning. In the four weeks before the flyby, mission controllers made just one small course correction. They had set aside six possible opportunities to make adjustments.

Angela Dietz, Juice’s spacecraft operations manager, said the team’s planning helped it use only a small amount of the fuel reserved for the flyby. Saving that fuel leaves more available for observations of Jupiter’s icy moons.

The Earth visit also gave scientists a chance to check Juice’s instruments. Calibration means checking and adjusting instruments so their measurements can be used reliably. Earth provided a familiar planet for these tests.

Teams spent months planning activities with the groups responsible for Juice’s 10 scientific instruments. They had to decide how to use the spacecraft’s available time, power and other resources.

Juice project scientist Claire Vallat explained that the journey offers only a few chances to test the instruments under well-understood conditions. When Juice passed through Earth’s shadow, it relied on battery power alone. The teams gave priority to tests that would help prepare the instruments for Jupiter.

The spacecraft also spent several days travelling through Earth’s magnetotail. This is the long part of Earth’s magnetic field that stretches away from the Sun.

Juice is scheduled to make 35 flybys of Jupiter’s moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. Planning for those encounters began years ago. Its Europa visits are expected in the early 2030s.

The Earth flyby served as a rehearsal, helping scientists learn how the instruments work in space and prepare to study future measurements. Controllers are continuing their close tracking of Juice through October 10.
why_it_matters: The flyby conserved fuel for observations of Jupiter’s icy moons and gave scientists a chance to test instruments under familiar conditions before future encounters.
